findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the benchmark-escape premise: CI does not exclude via `-m "not benchmark"` (default suite runs `-m "not integration and not external"`; existing benchmark tests use `skipif(CI=='true')`). Either add `not benchmark` to the CI marker filter, require the `skipif(CI)` guard alongside the marker, or drop the benchmark escape and adjust the teaching message + AC accordingly.
evidence: .github/workflows/_build-and-test.yml:469: `pytest -m "not integration and not external"` — no `not benchmark`
Grep for `not benchmark` across .github, Makefile, pyproject.toml returns no CI-invocation hit; only test docstrings at tests/scripts/reducer/test_reducer_cache.py:258,311 mention it aspirationally

tests/scripts/reducer/test_reducer_cache.py:246-248 shows the ACTUAL exclusion mechanism is `@pytest.mark.skipif(os.environ.get('CI')=='true', reason='Wall-clock benchmark skipped on CI runners')`, not a marker filter
pyproject.toml:587 registers `benchmark` as 'informational; not a pass/fail gate' but does not add it to addopts exclusion (addopts at :576 is only `--strict-markers --strict-config`)
findings.finding: The plan asserts `@pytest.mark.benchmark` is 'existing perf-lane convention, CI-excluded via -m "not benchmark"' and sanctions it as one of two escapes, but no CI invocation in the repo uses `-m "not benchmark"`. The default suite runs `pytest -m "not integration and not external"` (_build-and-test.yml:469) and the existing benchmark tests are excluded by an explicit `@pytest.mark.skipif(os.environ.get('CI')=='true')` guard, not by a benchmark marker filter. A wall-clock test carrying only `@pytest.mark.benchmark` would still run in default CI and still be exposed to the contention flake the detector exists to prevent.
findings.location: Approach section ('Escapes: ... or @pytest.mark.benchmark (existing perf-lane convention, CI-excluded via -m 'not benchmark')') and AC line 1
scenarios: An author marks a flaky upper-bound wall-clock test `@pytest.mark.benchmark` to satisfy the detector; the detector goes silent but the test still runs in the default CI cell and continues to flake under runner contention.
AC line 1 requires the teaching message to name both escapes, but one named escape does not actually remove the test from the flake-prone CI run.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the 'CI-excluded via -m "not benchmark"' assertion: verify/register the benchmark marker in pyproject.toml AND add the '-m "not benchmark"' exclusion to the CI workflow, or specify the actual exclusion mechanism (e.g. the skipif(CI) idiom the existing benchmark tests use).
evidence: No '-m "not benchmark"' occurrence in .github (search returned no matches)
'benchmark' not registered under pyproject.toml markers (no match)

tests/scripts/reducer/test_reducer_cache.py:245-249 actual CI exclusion is @pytest.mark.skipif(os.environ.get('CI')=='true', ...), with the -m 'not benchmark' mechanism described only aspirationally in the docstring
findings.finding: The plan makes an unverified capability assertion that is contradicted by the prior art it cites: it claims @pytest.mark.benchmark is 'CI-excluded via -m \'not benchmark\''. No .github workflow invokes '-m "not benchmark"', and 'benchmark' is not a registered marker in pyproject.toml. The only existing benchmark-marked tests (tests/scripts/reducer/test_reducer_cache.py) are actually excluded by @pytest.mark.skipif(os.environ.get('CI')=='true'), not by the runner flag. So a test carrying only @pytest.mark.benchmark (the plan's escape) would still run in CI, defeating the escape's purpose.
findings.location: Approach ('@pytest.mark.benchmark (existing perf-lane convention, CI-excluded via -m \'not benchmark\')')
scenarios: A test author uses @pytest.mark.benchmark as the plan-sanctioned escape; because CI never passes -m 'not benchmark', the wall-clock assert still executes on contended runners and flakes — the exact class the detector is meant to eliminate
findings.suggested_fix: Either wire '-m "not benchmark"' into .github/workflows/_build-and-test.yml and register the marker in pyproject.toml [tool.pytest.ini_options].markers, or change the documented escape to match the working prior art (@pytest.mark.skipif(os.environ.get('CI')=='true')) used in tests/scripts/reducer/test_reducer_cache.py.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the hang-guard marker's binding contract to its assert (e.g. immediately-preceding or same-line, one marker exempts exactly one assert) so the detector still fires on NEW unescaped upper-bound asserts in an already-marked file.
evidence: Approach: "Escapes: '# timing: hang-guard — <reason>' line marker" — no adjacency/same-line/scope rule stated
AC-1 goal is to block NEW asserts; a file-scoped marker would exempt not-yet-written asserts in an already-marked file
Mechanism-completeness: whether the guard actually blocks new asserts depends on the marker-to-assert binding, which the plan text leaves unresolved
findings.finding: The '# timing: hang-guard — <reason>' escape marker has no specified placement/association contract to the assert it exempts; if a single marker anywhere in a file (or loosely nearby) suppresses detection, it can silence unrelated FUTURE upper-bound asserts in the same file, undermining the detector's goal of blocking NEW unescaped asserts (AC-1).
findings.location: Plan 'Approach' section; AC-1 ('Detector blocks new unescaped upper-bound wall-clock asserts')
scenarios: A future PR adds a second, genuinely-flaky upper-bound assert to a file that already carries one hang-guard marker; the detector stays silent because the file already 'has a marker'
Reviewer cannot tell whether a marker's reason justifies the specific assert it is supposedly attached to
findings.suggested_fix: State that the marker must be on the line immediately preceding (or trailing) the specific upper-bound assert and exempts only that assert; a marker with no adjacent qualifying assert is itself a finding. Add a detector unit test: two asserts in one file, one marked → the unmarked one still fires.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a detector unit-test assertion that the fire message names both escape mechanisms ('# timing: hang-guard' and '@pytest.mark.benchmark').

AC4: 'covering fire, both escapes, and lower-bound exclusion' — message content unmeasured
findings.finding: AC line 1 requires the detector to emit 'a teaching message naming both escapes', but the detector unit-test AC (line 4) covers only fire / both-escape-silence / lower-bound-exclusion — no criterion asserts the teaching message content is present and names both escapes.
scenarios: Detector fires with an empty or unhelpful message; AC4 still passes
findings.suggested_fix: Extend the fire-case unit test to assert the emitted message string contains both escape tokens.

evidence: 1 criterion line(s) bundle multiple deliverables with 'and' (split so each is independently verifiable).

scripts/check_comment_hygiene.py is wired into .github/workflows/_build-and-test.yml:130; check_config_reads.py wired at :441
check_comment_hygiene.py has companion tests/unit/test_comment_hygiene_guard.py — same detector+unit-test shape the plan proposes
Plan quote: 'Seed implementation from /tmp/exp4_detector.py' — an out-of-tree prototype rather than the in-repo check_*.py pattern
findings.finding: The plan reinvents an established repo pattern without acknowledging it: the codebase already has a family of tree-scanning guard lints (scripts/check_comment_hygiene.py, check_criteria_vocabulary.py, check_config_reads.py, check_commit_message_wrap.py) that share the exact idiom the detector needs — SCANNED_TREES, EXCLUDED_FILES escape/allowlist, a check(root) entrypoint, CI wiring in _build-and-test.yml, and a companion tests/unit/test_*_guard.py. The plan instead says to 'Seed implementation from /tmp/exp4_detector.py' (an out-of-tree prototype) and only vaguely cites 'gate conventions', never naming this prior art as the template.
findings.location: Approach / Scope ('detector as DET code-review criterion ... or CI lint per gate conventions'; 'Seed implementation from /tmp/exp4_detector.py')

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify the regex approach against the repo's established AST-based guard convention (ast.parse in check_comment_hygiene.py / check_config_reads.py), or adopt AST parsing so the detector is robust to multiline asserts, helper-wrapped comparisons, and string-literal false surfaces.
evidence: scripts/check_comment_hygiene.py:178 tree = ast.parse(source)
scripts/check_config_reads.py:50,92 ast.parse(...) — established AST-based scanning convention
Plan quote: 'Detector prototype (regex + escapes) caught all, 0 FPs'
findings.finding: The plan chooses a regex-based detector ('regex + escapes') without justifying it against the repo's established AST-based guard approach. Sibling guards parse the AST (ast.parse in check_comment_hygiene.py and check_config_reads.py); a regex scanner over tests/** for upper-bound asserts is more brittle to multiline asserts, comparisons behind helper calls, and comparisons inside string literals — the very robustness the AST idiom exists to provide.
scenarios: A future upper-bound assert spans multiple lines or hides the comparison inside a helper/pytest.approx, evading a line-oriented regex and silently passing the gate
